content: In the United States, a study utilized 32 anti-HDV positive and 55 anti-HDV negative samples, as determined by reference assays, to evaluate diagnostic performance. Commercial ELISA kits have demonstrated reproducibility and feasibility across laboratories. In 2012, a French national control study for HDV diagnosis surveyed 24 laboratories, primarily in France but also in other parts of Europe and the USA. These laboratories used commercial ELISA kits, including DiaSorin (n=20), Adaltis (n=2), and DiaPro Diagnostic BioProbes (n=2). Using a panel of three positive and one negative sample, all laboratories achieved 100% concordance in identifying results. Another ELISA kit developed by General Biological Corporation (GB), initially a laboratory-developed kit and later commercialized, showed adequate clinical performance when compared to two existing commercial assays (DiaPro and DiaSorin ELISA). The GB HDV Ab kit, now commercialized with TFDA approval, demonstrated comparable results to the discontinued ETI-AB-DELTAK-2 (DiaSorin) and HDV Ab (DiaPro) kits. Among 913 HBsAg-positive serum samples, 86 tested positive on DiaPro, with an additional 15 positive on DiaSorin (101 total positives across both assays) and 108 total positives on GB. For 462 EDTA-treated plasma samples, 26 were positive on DiaPro, with an additional 4 positive on DiaSorin (30 positives across both assays) and 38 total positives on GB. The GB kit demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity compared to DiaPro and DiaSorin kits. A rapid diagnostic test for anti-HDV, developed as a simple lateral flow assay using a novel recombinant pan-genotypic large HDV antigen, provided results within 20 minutes using serum or plasma samples. This test was evaluated using 474 HBsAg-positive reference samples, including 332 anti-HDV positive samples (representing all genotypes except HDV-4) and 142 anti-HDV negative samples. The rapid test demonstrated high specificity compared to commercial enzyme immunoassays (DiaPro and DiaSorin). However, 18 samples that tested negative on the rapid test but positive on reference EIA had very low HDV titers and either unknown or negative RNA status. Nucleic acid assays for HDV RNA have shown variability in performance, particularly with non-HDV-1 strains (e.g., African strains and genotypes 5–8). A 2016 international external quality control study for HDV RNA quantification in plasma samples highlighted these challenges. The study involved 28 laboratories across 17 countries, with most using in-house assays and six using commercial assays. The first panel included 20 clinical samples of various genotypes (1, 2, and 5–8) and two negative samples. The second panel consisted of dilutions of the WHO HDV international standard to enable standardization of comparisons across laboratories. Laboratories using primers and probes targeting the conserved ribozyme region performed better. However, some laboratories underestimated RNA viral load or failed to detect RNA in certain genotypes, and two laboratories reported false positives in negative controls. Commercially available assays for HDV RNA quantification, such as EurobioPlex (CE-IVD) and in-house assays developed at the French National Reference Laboratory (FNRL), have shown comparable results. A study using 611 clinical samples across all HDV genotypes demonstrated 97.7% sensitivity for EurobioPlex. However, 14 samples identified as RNA-positive by EurobioPlex were negative on the FNRL assay. Among 105 anti-HDV negative samples positive for other hepatitis viruses, EurobioPlex demonstrated 100% specificity, identifying all as HDV RNA negative. Automated solutions for HDV RNA testing, such as the HDV utility channel assay developed for the Roche cobas 6800 system, have shown strong analytical and clinical performance. In an evaluation using 20 samples from an external quality assessment panel, the assay correctly identified all qualitative samples (16/16 positive, 4/4 negative). However, automated nucleic acid extraction methods, such as those using AmpliPrep, MagNA Pure, and QIAcube systems, yielded lower HDV RNA viral loads compared to manual extraction methods. Despite advancements, testing for HDV among individuals with chronic HBV infection remains limited, and HDV diagnosis has not been prioritized in public health programming. Current diagnostic options include total anti-HDV screening followed by HDV RNA testing to confirm active infection. HDV has eight genotypes with significant genetic variability and geographic distribution, posing challenges for assay standardization. There are limited commercially available options for anti-HDV and HDV RNA assays, and no gold standard assays exist. This lack of standardization complicates the demonstration of diagnostic accuracy for assays. Future research should focus on evaluating diagnostic performance across genotypes and populations, developing international reference standards for non-HDV-1 genotypes, and exploring promising investigational methods, such as rapid diagnostic tests, to decentralize screening. Aligning on the importance of HDV diagnosis in public health programming may stimulate demand for and development of commercialized HDV diagnostic products.
